paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Iron fertilization is any process, natural or deliberate, that adds iron back to the upper ocean. Iron can boost the growth of phytoplankton, which take carbon dioxide (CO₂) out of the air through photosynthesis. Phytoplankton are the primary producers of the sea: the rest of the marine food web feeds on them.

paragraphs.heading: Why iron runs short
paragraphs.text: All life needs iron, and plants need it for photosynthesis. Yet the upper ocean holds so little that nobody managed to measure it until the 1980s. Iron mostly does not dissolve in seawater and sinks easily. Across much of the ocean, it is the limiting nutrient, the one that holds back phytoplankton growth. About a quarter of the ocean surface has plenty of major nutrients but little plant life, and these high-nutrient low-chlorophyll (HNLC) waters are held back mainly by trace nutrients, especially iron.

paragraphs.heading: Nature's iron deliveries
paragraphs.text: Iron-rich minerals reach the sea in wind-blown dust, volcanic ash, rivers and glaciers. Upwelling currents can carry nutrient-rich sediment to the surface. Whales help too: they eat iron-rich organisms in deep water and then defecate at the surface, feeding phytoplankton blooms. Fewer sperm whales in the Southern Ocean has been linked to 200,000 tonnes a year less carbon being taken from the air, possibly because phytoplankton grew less.

paragraphs.heading: Where the carbon goes
paragraphs.text: Phytoplankton need sunlight and nutrients, and as they grow they take up CO₂ and lock its carbon into their tissue. When they die, some of that carbon sinks deep into the ocean. Much of it can instead be eaten by other organisms, such as small fish and zooplankton. Carbon that reaches the deep ocean can stay there for hundreds or thousands of years, but carbon that does not sink far enough may rise and return to the air.

paragraphs.heading: Iron and the ice ages
paragraphs.text: In the late 1980s, oceanographer John Martin put forward the iron hypothesis, drawing on Antarctic ice cores and his own experiments. He showed that adding iron to iron-poor seawater can set off huge phytoplankton blooms that pull down a great deal of CO₂ from the air. He also found that more iron-rich dust blowing off the continents was behind much of the CO₂ drop that cooled the planet before ice ages.

paragraphs.heading: Testing it on purpose
paragraphs.text: Since 1990, 13 major large-scale experiments have tested how well iron fertilization works and what it might do. All of them saw more phytoplankton growth when tiny amounts of iron were added. In one trial, EIFEX, at least half the bloom sank below 1,000 metres, likely locking its carbon away for hundreds or thousands of years. Critics worry about side effects on a marine ecosystem we only partly understand. Researchers reply that no harm has been seen in field trials, though scientists still call for careful monitoring.
